newsitem.title: MEXICO: Pemex blast is latest in string of fatal mishaps.
newsitem.headline: Pemex blast is latest in string of fatal mishaps.

text.p: Monday's inferno at a fuel storage facility was the latest in a string of fatal disasters at installations owned by Mexico's state-owned oil giant Pemex, whose safety record has been repeatedly attacked by Mexican media and opposition politicians.

Pemex is one of the world's biggest oil companies, producing about 2.85 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil. It generates huge wealth for the Mexican treasury but critics say it has at times cut corners on safety.

Only four months ago, a huge Pemex gas processing plant at Cactus in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas blew up, killing six workers and starting a huge blaze that caused millions of dollars worth of damage. An investigation concluded that operators had blundered.

"Just after the blast, there were reports that a recent inspection of a Pemex gasoline pipeline passing through the Cactus complex revealed 2,099 anomalies," the Latin American Energy Alert newsletter said in September.

"Pemex has had a number of major accidents in recent years that either resulted in heavy loss of life and property or severe damage to the environment. In most cases, subsequent investigations revealed problems with the company's maintenance regime or operational practices," it added.

In February, opposition activists blockaded more than 20 oil wells in one of Pemex's main oil producing areas, the southeastern state of Tabasco. They protested that constant Pemex oil spills had turned their once-lush and beautiful tropical state into a barren wasteland.
A Pemex pipeline in the state blew up in February 1994, killing at least six people. The corporation later acknowledged a lack of adequate attention to normal maintenance procedures.
But those unlucky incidents pale beside Pemex's worst mishap of recent years. In April 1992, gasoline leaked from Pemex pipelines into the sewer system of Mexico's second biggest city Guadalajara.
The ensuing string of explosions tore up whole streets and killed more than 200 people. Several top Pemex officials were jailed for criminal negligence but later released.
San Juan Ixhuatepec, the site of Monday's inferno, is no stranger to energy accidents either.

Mexicans remember the town as the site of one of their worst ever recent disasters, when a liquefied petroleum gas storage depot owned by a private company blew up, sending tongues of flame into hundreds of surrounding houses and burning 511 people to death.

Residents' protests and demands to move dangerous oil and gas facilities away from residential areas were not heeded. Six years later, a Pemex fuel line there ignited in a ball of fire, killing at least one worker. Pemex employees claimed three other men and even gave their names but the oil giant denied the fatalities -- and still refused to move the facilities.
The oil giant has had problems on the high seas too. In June 1995, one of its oil tankers suffered an explosion and caught fire, killing two people.
